item.title: Kodak Black Confirmed For GTA VI As Role Stays Under Wraps
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kodak Black and Bradford Cohen confirmed his GTA VI appearance, adding a clear new fact to Rockstar's unnamed launch image.
item.content:encoded:
Kodak Black has confirmed that he appears in Grand Theft Auto VI, adding the artist’s own word to a launch image that Rockstar Games published without a caption.

Kodak and his attorney, Bradford Cohen, confirmed the appearance in a social media video.

That confirmation adds the key detail confirming AllHipHop’s November 6 coverage of Rockstar’s launch gallery. At the time, the official image showed a man whose face tattoos, hair and 1800 Block chain closely resembled the Pompano Beach rapper.

Rockstar did not name the figure, and Kodak had not publicly described his involvement.

Rockstar released the gallery on November 5 as part of the final two-week push toward the game’s November 19 launch. Its announcement directed fans to a larger collection of screenshots from Vice City and the wider state of Leonida, but it did not identify the people shown in those images.

Kodak’s confirmation strengthens the identification but doesn’t fill in the rest of the picture.

Rockstar has not announced a character name, credited him as a voice actor or described a mission tied to his appearance.

The South Florida connection gives the cameo a natural setting. Kodak, whose legal name is Bill Kapri, is from Pompano Beach.

GTA VI returns the series to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, and expands the map across a Florida-inspired state.

The studio has used regional music, landmarks and nightlife throughout the rollout. Kodak’s music was already connected to the game before the gallery appeared, but the new confirmation places the rapper himself inside the world Rockstar has built.

Players will get their first chance to see how much of Kodak’s appearance survived into the finished game when Grand Theft Auto VI arrives November 19.

item.title: Donald Trump Says He Would Rather Go To Hell Than Forgive His Enemies
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Donald Trump told 60 Minutes he may never forgive some political enemies, even under a hypothetical tied to heaven.
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump said he may never forgive some political enemies, even when asked to imagine that forgiveness as the final condition for entering heaven.

The exchange came during Trump’s first post-midterm interview with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat. The president said he considered himself religious, hoped to reach heaven and did not want to go to hell.

Douthat then offered a pointed hypothetical. He asked whether Trump could forgive figures such as former FBI Director James Comey and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi if paradise depended on it.

Trump described those opponents as dishonest and harmful to the country. He cited his indictments, two impeachments and what he called the weaponization of government before answering.

“I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies and I always will,” Trump said.

The question built on Trump’s remarks at Charlie Kirk’s September 2025 memorial service in Arizona. Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, had spoken about forgiving the man accused of killing her husband. Trump later told the crowd that Charlie Kirk wanted the best for his opponents, while he did not share that view.

That earlier line drew laughter at the memorial and was widely treated as a blunt description of Trump’s political style. More than a year later, Douthat returned to it as a question about faith, judgment and whether the president could separate personal grievance from Christian forgiveness.

Trump did not soften the answer. He said giving an easy yes would feel false, then argued that love of country outweighed any obligation he felt toward people he viewed as destructive.

Douthat pressed him by pointing to the success and advantages Trump had received during his life. The president still declined to promise forgiveness.

The full interview covered Republican midterm losses, immigration, the economy, Iran, Ukraine and possible successors to the MAGA movement. The forgiveness exchange stood apart because it placed Trump’s familiar complaints about political foes inside a religious test he accepted on his own terms.

Trump treated the hypothetical as a question about his own willingness to forgive before final judgment. His response left little ambiguity about the grudge itself.

item.title: EU Presses TikTok To Redesign Its “For You” Feed
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: TikTok's For You feed faces an EU redesign demand after regulators flagged harmful recommendation loops and weak user controls.
item.content:encoded:
TikTok is facing a European demand to rebuild parts of its For You feed after regulators said its recommendation system can pull users into repeated loops of harmful content.

The European Commission issued preliminary findings under the Digital Services Act, focusing on what it calls the feed’s “rabbit hole effect.”

The regulator said watching or liking certain videos can prompt TikTok to serve more of the same, including material about sadness, isolation, weight loss and body image.

Commission officials said TikTok did not adequately assess those risks or put effective safeguards in place, particularly for minors and vulnerable adults.

The proposed fixes reach into the feed’s basic machinery: give more weight to a user’s stated preferences, stop using viewing time as a recommendation signal, make controls easier to use and regularly test the algorithm.

The findings are preliminary.

TikTok can review the Commission’s evidence and respond before regulators make a final decision. A confirmed violation could expose parent company ByteDance to a fine of up to 6 percent of its global annual revenue.

TikTok rejected the Commission’s account in a statement to Reuters.

“The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety,” the company said.

For artists and listeners, the practical stakes sit in the distribution system. TikTok’s feed decides which clips surface repeatedly and which ones fall away, so changing the signals behind those recommendations could alter how music, dances and cultural conversations travel through the platform.

The Commission’s requested changes focus on recommendation inputs and user controls rather than individual songs or creators.

The case is part of a longer review of TikTok’s design.

In February, the Commission separately issued preliminary findings on features including infinite scroll, autoplay and push notifications. In July, it said the platform’s protections for minors also fell short of the Digital Services Act.

This latest stage narrows the dispute to the way the For You feed learns from engagement and repeats similar subjects. TikTok now has to answer the regulator’s evidence while the Commission decides whether those design changes become an enforceable order.

item.title: Common Meets A Miami Orchestra For One Night At The Arsht
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Common will perform with Miami's Nu Deco Ensemble in a one-night Arsht Center program built around new orchestral arrangements.
item.content:encoded:
Common will bring his catalog into a different setting in Miami on Thursday, November 12, joining Nu Deco Ensemble for a one-night performance at the Adrienne Arsht Center’s Knight Concert Hall.

The program puts a live orchestra behind music drawn from more than three decades of Hip-Hop, film and theater work.

Nu Deco co-founder and artistic director Sam Hyken will conduct the ensemble, which is known for building new arrangements around contemporary artists instead of treating orchestral backing as decoration.

Hyken has made clear that the collaboration comes from a long relationship with Common’s work. “Like Water for Chocolate, Be, and Electric Circus are three of my all-time favorite hip-hop albums,” he told Miami New Times when the dates were announced.

The Miami concert is expected to include “Love of My Life” and “Glory,” the Oscar-winning song Common recorded with John Legend for Selma. It will also draw from a career that recently added The Auditorium: Vol. 1, his 2024 full-length collaboration with Pete Rock.

That album earned Grammy nominations for Best Rap Album and Best Rap Performance.

Nu Deco was founded in Miami in 2015 and built its identity around collaborations that move across classical music, Hip-Hop, soul, jazz and pop. Its previous guests include Wyclef Jean, Macy Gray, Stephen Marley, Bilal, Masego and Emily King.

The organization says its concerts and recordings have reached more than 100,000 audience members and 15 million streams.

Its education work has served more than 174,000 students, while Nu Deco Access has distributed thousands of free tickets in Miami-Dade County.

That local history gives the Arsht date more weight than a standard tour stop. Common is not arriving with a traveling backing band or a fixed festival set.

The performance centers on Nu Deco’s sound and how its musicians reinterpret a guest’s existing material.

The Knight Concert Hall show begins at 8 p.m. and is scheduled to run about 90 to 100 minutes. Common and Nu Deco will take the same collaboration to Orlando’s Walt Disney Theater the following night, but Miami gets the first performance and the orchestra’s home stage.

item.title: Mello Buckzz’s Gun Plea Adds Concurrent Two-Year Prison Term
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Mello Buckzz pleaded guilty in her Chicago gun case and received a two-year term running with her existing sentence.
item.content:encoded:
Mello Buckzz received a two-year prison sentence after pleading guilty in a Chicago gun case, adding a complete outcome to a legal development that had previously remained unresolved.

The artist, whose legal name is Melanie Doyle, pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a weapon before Judge William Gamboney. The judge imposed a two-year term that will run at the same time as another two-year sentence Judge Patrick Coughlin issued in her aggravated battery case.

AllHipHop previously reported the battery sentence and the October 26 court entry in the separate gun matter. At that point, the weapons case’s full disposition had not been established.

The gun prosecution followed Mello Buckzz’s June 15 traffic stop in Chicago. Police alleged that officers saw illegal windshield tint before finding suspected marijuana in her purse, an open alcohol container inside the vehicle and a handgun beneath the driver’s seat.

Officers also accused her of refusing repeated instructions to leave the vehicle.

Prosecutors initially charged Mello Buckzz with aggravated unlawful possession of a weapon, along with two misdemeanor counts of resisting or obstructing an officer. Police said the recovered Glock 43X was loaded and had been reported stolen in Bedford Park.

The plea was for felon in possession of a weapon.

Mello Buckzz was already on probation when police arrested her in June. She had pleaded guilty in April 2025 to aggravated battery in a public place. Different judges imposed the later prison sentence and the gun sentence, but the concurrent structure means the terms run together rather than one after the other.

CWB Chicago reported that Mello Buckzz was transferred from Cook County custody to Logan Correctional Center on November 4.

The outlet cited Illinois Department of Corrections records listing June 2 as her projected release date after sentence reduction.

Mello Buckzz drew national attention after her mixtape release party was shot up, leaving four people dead and 18 wounded.

item.title: Eazy The Block Captain Accused Of Using Ghostwriter As Former Friend SCO Makes Explosive Claims
item.dc:creator: illseed
item.description: Eazy The Block Captain faces stunning ghostwriting allegations from former friend, who claims he helped write some of the battle rapper's most memorable bars.
item.content:encoded:
What in the hell is going on?


Eazy The Block Captain may have opened a door he wishes he had kept closed, because a former friend is now questioning the authenticity of his celebrated battle rap pen.

The Philadelphia rapper has spent weeks stirring up controversy over his claims that he helped write material for Tsu Surf. That has our heads spinning!

During an October 26 episode of The Real Report, the hosts discussed Eazy’s reported claim that he wrote as much as half of Surf’s rounds, including material connected to battles against John John Da Don and Cortez. 

Tsu Surf has pushed back. In an October 15 discussion circulated by HipHopIsReal, Surf challenged Eazy’s account and argued that teammates exchanging feedback is fundamentally different from someone writing another battler’s rou

Now, in a wild UNO reverse, a former battle rapper known as SCO has emerged with allegations that could make Eazy reconsider the wisdom of discussing other people’s writing habits.

According to claims circulated by BattleRapDose, SCO alleges that he helped Eazy write material for almost every battle throughout his career. Not just a clever punchline here or a little creative assistance there. SCO is reportedly claiming involvement in some of the haymakers that helped establish Eazy as a formidable force in battle rap.

That is quite an accusation.

SCO reportedly pointed to Eazy’s battle against John John Da Don as one example. He also allegedly named Muuwop, an artist formerly associated with Eazy’s Trenches operation, as someone who witnessed part of the writing process.

Those claims have not been independently substantiated, and Muuwop has not publicly corroborated the account in the material reviewed.

But the timing is crazy.

Eazy recently caused an uproar by claiming he contributed substantial material to Tsu Surf’s rounds. And Murda Mook and other battle rap veterans have debated whether exchanging ideas constitutes ghostwriting. There’s a distinction, but there be hypocrisy between as well.

And now SCO is essentially turning Eazy’s own argument against him.

Battle rap is a peculiar place. Rappers can threaten each other’s relatives, invent outrageous criminal scenarios and say things that would make a sailor blush. But suggest somebody else wrote their bars? Suddenly, everybody loses their minds!

There is a significant distinction between helping a friend refine a punchline and secretly writing entire rounds. SCO’s allegations do not establish which, if either, occurred. But sounds like he doubles down on the help part.

As of this writing, Eazy has not issued a response specifically addressing SCO’s latest allegations.

If battle rappers have been quietly helping each other construct their most celebrated performances, how much of the culture’s competitive mythology needs reconsideration? I think it’s time, like reconsidering what’s snitching.

The bigger question is whether SCO has receipts. I want to see them.

Because accusations make headlines, but evidence can change legacies.

What do you think?

item.title: Paid In Full Grants Help Hip-Hop Pioneers Buy Homes & Cover Medical Bills
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Paid In Full's five-year grants have helped Hip-Hop pioneers buy homes, cover medical bills and finish delayed creative work.
item.content:encoded:
The Paid In Full Foundation‘s five-year grants are helping Hip-Hop pioneers buy homes, cover medical bills and complete creative projects delayed for years.

Those results move the foundation’s work beyond an awards-night promise.

A November 7 Weekend Culture report for a16z by Jeff Weiss examined what happened after recipients began receiving the no-strings support attached to the Hip Hop Grandmaster Awards.

Grandmaster Caz offered the clearest measure of that impact. The Cold Crush Brothers MC was still living in public housing when his first Paid In Full checks arrived, according to the report.

Other recipients have used their grants to purchase homes, settle medical expenses and return to unfinished work.

“Hip-hop has no social security,” Caz said.

His point reaches back to the business history behind “Rapper’s Delight.”

Caz wrote lyrics later performed on the hit by Big Bank Hank, but he did not receive songwriting credit or royalties for that contribution. His influence traveled farther than the money did.

Ben and Felicia Horowitz built Paid In Full around that imbalance.

Each honoree receives an unconditional grant spread across five years, giving recipients room to make decisions based on their own needs. Ben Horowitz described the idea through the value he received from Eric B. & Rakim’s Paid in Full: “I bought it for $10 and got at least $5 million worth of value out of it.”

A September conversation with Caz, Nas, Steve Stoute and Horowitz explained why the program combines money with public recognition.

The group argued that financial help alone could not replace the credit many foundational artists missed while Hip-Hop became a global business.

AllHipHop’s recent coverage tracked the public side of that work.

The October 24 gala honored Kurtis Blow and The D.O.C. as Grandmasters, while Nile Rodgers received the Quincy Jones Achievement Award and Ralph McDaniels received the Contributor Award.

The event report also noted a five-year, $500,000 grant within this year’s program.

The November report adds the part that a ceremony cannot show. When recipients turn the grants into stable housing, paid medical care and completed music, the foundation’s idea of repayment becomes something that can be measured in their daily lives.

item.title: Russell Brand Gets 10.5 Years & Indefinite Sex-Offender Reporting
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Russell Brand received 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assaults, with indefinite sex-offender reporting after release.
item.content:encoded:
Russell Brand received a 10-year, six-month prison sentence on November 9 for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, with sex-offender reporting requirements set to continue indefinitely after his release.

At Southwark Crown Court, Judge Joel Bennathan gave the 51-year-old nine years for rape and separate sexual assault sentences of nine months, 18 months and eight months. The assault terms will run together, with the longest added to the rape sentence.

Brand had denied all seven charges. A jury convicted him on November 5 and cleared him of two other rape charges and one charge of attempted indecent assault. The four convictions concerned crimes committed between 2004 and 2009.

In his sentencing remarks, Judge Bennathan explained how he applied the totality principle, which requires an overall punishment to be just and proportionate.

“In practice that guidance means I should not make all four sentences consecutive to one another, and I should consider reducing one or more of the individual terms of imprisonment,” Judge Bennathan said. “I will, of course, follow that guidance but you committed sexual offences against a number of women over a five-year period: If I were to make all the sentences concurrent or greatly reduce any of them, that would not do justice to the overall gravity of your criminality.”

Judge Bennathan described the lasting harm in the rape victim’s impact statement.

“In her victim impact statement she wrote of struggling to eat and sleep, of taking two to three months off from work and of abandoning the career she had embarked upon. Although the rape was 17 years ago, she still finds it affects her ability to form new friendships and to know when she can trust people,” he said.

He also stressed that the women’s choices did not reduce Brand’s culpability: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.”

Reuters footage below covers the November 5 verdict.

The court also weighed Brand’s conduct since the crimes against the seriousness of the offenses.

“The mitigation in your case is the fact you had no significant previous convictions, and the 17 years that have passed since the last of these offences, and the life you have led since, doing good work and especially in assisting those wrestling with addictions, often by funding treatment,” Judge Bennathan said.

He noted that sentencing guidelines limit the weight given to good character in serious sexual offenses, then explained his decision: “Nonetheless, in my view it would be wrong to disregard your mitigation all together, so I will reduce the sentence I would otherwise have imposed for the rape by a year.”

Prosecutors argued that Brand’s fame worsened the harm because the women kept seeing him in public coverage and helped him commit the crimes. Judge Bennathan distinguished those two points.

“I have taken the first aspect into account in assessing the harm you caused but I regard the second as an intrinsic part of each offence. I also need to be careful I am not punishing you more because you are famous,” he said.

Judge Bennathan also explained why he had not ordered a pre-sentence report.

“These crimes are far too serious for anything other than immediate custody, and given how long ago these offences were committed and the evidence of your wife, I accept there is no sound evidential basis for me to conclude you pose a risk for the future,” Judge Bennathan said.

Brand will receive credit for the days he has already spent in custody. Judge Bennathan also set out what follows prison.

“You will serve two thirds of that sentence then be released on licence and will be liable to be recalled into custody if you breach its terms. On your release you will also be indefinitely subject to the notification requirements under the Sexual Offences Act 2003.”

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Kanye West & Ty Dolla $ign Sued Over “Vultures” Sample Sent By Text
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: Kanye West and Ty Dolla $ign faced a lawsuit alleging an MP3 shared for a possible collaboration became "Vultures" without a deal.
item.content:encoded:
Kanye West and Ty Dolla $ign were sued by two producers who alleged that an MP3 shared for a possible collaboration became the foundation of “Vultures” without a license or payment.

Jae Deal and Marlon “Marlonwiththeglasses” Barrow filed their copyright complaint in federal court in California. They named Ye, Ty Dolla $ign, Yeezy Record Label LLC, Yeezy LLC and Create Music Group as defendants.

Their account traces the dispute to “Joint 2,” a recording and composition they said they created together in November 2018 and owned in equal shares. The lawsuit also covers five separately mixed audio files, known as stems.

According to the 24-page complaint, Ty Dolla $ign heard the music playing during a phone call with Barrow, a longtime friend and collaborator. He asked to visit Barrow’s studio and later requested a copy for a possible album.

Barrow sent an MP3 by text. The producers said he held back the stems and higher-quality files until the parties signed an agreement covering use of the music.

They alleged that Ty Dolla $ign then shared the MP3 with Ye and that versions of “Vultures” reached commercial platforms in November 2023 before any licensing deal was negotiated.

“Barrow was accorded a producer credit, but received no compensation whatsoever. Deal was never accorded a producer credit nor paid any compensation whatsoever,” the complaint stated.

The producers alleged that efforts to stop the releases began before Vultures 1 arrived in February 2024. Deal described takedown requests in December 2023 and a January 2024 discussion with producer 88-Keys, whom the complaint identified as Yeezy’s head of music.

During that exchange, Deal said he made clear that he had not assigned his rights or received payment. The complaint alleged that the music was nevertheless used again on the Vultures Pack EP, including the “Havoc Version,” and on Vultures 1.

Deal also described rejecting an October 2024 buyout offer and continuing to demand credit and compensation. The complaint did not give the offer’s amount.

The dispute extends to a July 9, 2025 copyright registration. The producers alleged that it omitted Deal as an author and falsely claimed Barrow had transferred his rights by contract. They maintained that no signed transfer agreement existed.

“This action is not only about unpaid licensing fees and the lack of appropriate credit, but also about the essential right of any artist to determine when, how, and by whom their creative work is used,” the complaint stated.

The filing follows other disputes over music used on the Vultures projects. Donna Summer’s estate reached a 2024 settlement over “Good (Don’t Die),” which was removed from Vultures 1.

More recently, a different producer sued Ye over allegedly unpaid AI vocal work on Vultures 2 and Bully. That case was filed in August and concerns different work and claims.

Deal and Barrow requested a jury trial, actual damages and profits attributable to the alleged infringement, or alternative statutory damages. They also asked for injunctions blocking further use of their work and an order covering copies and source materials used to reproduce it.

item.title: BigXthaPlug’s Top 10 Debut Follows Direct Fan Album Rollout
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: BigXthaPlug matches his Billboard 200 peak as Better Over Time follows an album campaign built around fan access and film.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas rapper BigXthaPlug has matched his Billboard 200 peak with Better Over Time, after a campaign that paired early fan access with a short film.

The album opens at No. 7 with 35,000 equivalent album units on the chart dated November 14, according to Billboard. That puts it alongside the No. 7 peak of his 2025 country project I Hope You’re Happy. His 2024 album Take Care reached No. 8.

The release took more than one form during its opening week.

The original October 30 edition contained 18 songs and ran 42 minutes. A November 2 version expanded the record to 19 songs and 45 minutes, adding the “LITE” remix with Lil Wayne and Belly Gang Kushington.

Before either edition arrived, BigX had opened a separate destination for fans to buy into the project. His branded EVEN STUDIO hub offered an album pre-order starting at $7.99, with early access to selected tracks.

The offer also included a community chat, merchandise access, behind-the-scenes videos and tour information.

That gave the campaign a place where listeners could follow the release beyond a streaming album page. The advance offer centered on the original 18-song tracklist, ahead of the October 30 release, through an exclusive license to UnitedMasters.

The film supplied another route into the music.

AllHipHop attended the October 26 Dallas preview at a Cinemark theater, where invited guests watched the short film and heard the album before its release. BigX followed the screening with a parking-lot performance, inviting fans to appear during a taping.

Earlier in the campaign, billboards in seven cities introduced the album’s guests in their hometowns. Memphis carried GloRilla’s image, Detroit featured Babyface Ray, and Dallas highlighted Ro$ama, connecting the collaborators with local audiences before the complete lineup was announced.

The album itself brought his collaborators together across several tracks.

Leon Thomas appears on “NO LIMIT,” Ava Max joins “BURN,” and GloRilla features on “FAF.” Babyface Ray and Lil Yachty share “BELIEVE,” while Fridayy appears on “HEAL ME.” The expanded edition keeps those records alongside the added Lil Wayne remix.
